findings.text: follow-on: 'assert elapsed < WORKER_SLEEP_SECONDS' can never fail. The preceding _wait_until returns only when the supervisor's pid is gone within CEILING_SECONDS (90s), and WORKER_SLEEP_SECONDS is 0.120e3, so elapsed < 90 < 120 always; when the escalation is withheld the wait itself raises first. The line reads as a second upper-bound guard but adds none -- the discriminator is the 90s ceiling sitting under the worker's own sleep. Same shape at line 299. Not harmful; noted so a later reader does not rely on it as a bound.

justifications.goal_fidelity: The done-when is met and I reproduced it. The recorded defect was a supervisor that survives a crew stop: its SIGTERM/SIGHUP handler only records the stop (the Event returned by _record_stop_before_spawn, dispatch.py:8512-8531), then the reap loop blocks in os.waitpid for as long as the worker lives, so a worker that ignores the group signal holds the supervisor (and its slot) unbounded. The merged head 798f3d107 bounds that wait inside the reap loop: _reap_worker_on_its_terminal_manifest now takes stop_requested and stop_grace_seconds (dispatch.py:8847-8848), and once the stop Event is set it re-signals the worker SIGTERM reason 'run-stop' then SIGKILL reason 'worker-ignored-the-stop-grace-signal' after the grace (dispatch.py:8903-8930); the single production caller _run_supervisor passes stop_requested (the pre-spawn handler Event) and _stop_grace_seconds() (dispatch.py:9088-9089). I confirmed the signal mask is restored in the finally at dispatch.py:9063-9064 before the reap loop, so a stop delivered during the reap fires the handler and sets the Event. The test launches a real detached supervisor over a SIGTERM-ignoring stub, stops the run via dispatch.terminate (the call crew stop makes), and asserts the supervisor's pid is gone within a bounded wait, the worker pid gone, the exit record written, and the sender record naming the kill. Re-ran at head in a scratch tree: 3 passed (node module) / 22 passed (four-module arm), EXIT=0.
